Alone
a-lone'
a. and adv. (single; without company; by itself only; rendering Hebrew bad and levad, Greek monos)
From all and one — al one, wholly by oneself. The same compound, worn down further, gives lone and lonely. Hebrew levad means in separation, apart.

Biblical Definition

Alone receives the first negative verdict in Scripture. In a creation repeatedly pronounced good, one thing is not: “It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him” (Genesis 2:18) — spoken before the fall, so human aloneness is a deficiency in the created order rather than a consequence of sin, and the remedy God provides is another person. Ecclesiastes reasons practically to the same conclusion: “if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up” (Ecclesiastes 4:10). The word also marks the limits of what will sustain a man. In the wilderness our Lord answers the first temptation: “It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4) — bread is not denied, it is denied the whole office. And the most searching use is his own, hours before the arrest: “the hour cometh, yea, is now come, that ye shall be scattered, every man to his own, and shall leave me alone: and yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me” (John 16:32). He states both facts without softening either. He was left alone by every friend, and he was not alone — until Golgotha, where he asked why he had been forsaken, so that his people never need to.

Webster 1828 Definition

Single; without company. It is the first thing in creation called not good; Ecclesiastes pities the man who falls alone; bread alone will not sustain a man; and Christ, left alone by all, says the Father is with him.

expand to see more

ALONE, a. [all and one.] Single; solitary; without the presence of another; applied to a person or thing.

2. It is applied to a person or thing which is by itself, or which excludes all others; as, God alone is holy.

3. ALONE, adv. Separately; by itself.

4. To let alone, to suffer to rest; to forbear molesting or meddling with.

5. In Scripture, it is not good that the man should be alone, Gen. 2; man shall not live by bread alone, Matt. 4.

Key Scripture

Genesis 2:18 — "And the LORD God said, It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him."

Matthew 4:4 — "But he answered and said, It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God."

Ecclesiastes 4:10 — "For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up."

John 16:32 — "Behold, the hour cometh, yea, is now come, that ye shall be scattered, every man to his own, and shall leave me alone: and yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me."

Modern Corruption

Isolation is chosen and called independence, against the first not good in Scripture — while the solas, which use the word rightly, are softened by adding something to faith, grace, Christ, Scripture, or God's glory.

expand to see more

Genesis 2:18 is a pre-fall verdict, and it settles a good deal. Man's need of others is not a weakness introduced by sin but a feature of how God made him, and the arrangements Scripture gives for it are marriage, family, and the local church — embodied, committed, and inconvenient. An age that can simulate company at any hour has made isolation comfortable enough to choose, and calls it independence. Ecclesiastes answers with a scene rather than an argument: a man falls, and there is nobody to lift him up. That is not a description of loneliness as an emotion but of a practical exposure, and it is why Hebrews commands the assembling of ourselves together and warns against the manner of some who forsake it. There is a right use of the word, and it is the Reformation's. Grace alone, faith alone, Christ alone, Scripture alone, to the glory of God alone — and in every case the word does its work by excluding. Add anything to any of the five and the doctrine is gone: faith plus merit is not faith alone, and Scripture plus tradition as a coordinate authority is not Scripture alone.

The principle to recover is John 16:32, which holds two things together that a believer must learn to hold. Christ says plainly that his friends will scatter and leave him alone, and in the same breath that he is not alone, because the Father is with him. Both are true, and the second does not cancel the sting of the first. That is the pattern for every Christian abandoned by those who should have stood by him. And there is one point at which the pattern does not transfer: on the cross he was forsaken by the Father too, and the cry of dereliction was uttered so that Hebrews could promise the rest of us I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew bad means separation, apart; levad, by oneself. Greek monos is alone, single, the root of monergism — God working alone in salvation.

expand to see more

Hebrew bad (H905) — separation, a part; the root of levad, alone.

Hebrew levad (H905) — by itself, alone; it is not good that the man should be alone.

Hebrew ezer kenegdo (H5828 with H5048) — a help meet for him; the remedy God provided.

Greek monos (G3441) — alone, only, single; the word in Matthew 4:4 and John 16:32.

Greek monogenes (G3439) — only begotten; the same root applied to the Son.

Usage

"Of the first thing called not good: it is not good that the man should be alone (Genesis 2:18)."

"Of what bread cannot do: man shall not live by bread alone (Matthew 4:4)."

"Of the Lord left and not left: shall leave me alone: and yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me (John 16:32)."
